name: Network Foundations
blurb: The path a Network+ syllabus takes, in the order the ideas actually build on each other: layers, then addressing, then the devices, then what breaks.
for: Anyone starting in IT, and anyone who has been faking subnetting for years.

name: SOC Analyst Starter
blurb: What a first-line analyst is actually asked to do, from the vocabulary through triage to the moment an alert becomes an incident.
for: Anyone heading for a Tier 1 seat, or interviewing for one.

name: First 90 Days on an Endpoint Team
blurb: Enrolment, policy, compliance and patching — the shape of a modern device estate, and the order a new engineer meets it in.
for: Someone joining an Intune, MECM or UEM team.

name: Cloud From Zero
blurb: Regions and responsibility first, then compute, storage, identity and the bill — the order that stops cloud from being a pile of product names.
for: Anyone whose employer just moved, or is about to.

name: Comfortable in the Terminal
blurb: From "which directory am I in" to writing something that runs on a schedule, without the detour through memorising flags.
for: Anyone who avoids the terminal, and anyone who uses it without enjoying it.

name: Breaking Into IT
blurb: The honest version: what the entry-level jobs are, what to learn first, what to build, and how to talk about it.
for: Career changers, students, and anyone applying without a degree in it.

name: Data From First Principles
blurb: Databases in the order the ideas build on each other: how one actually works, the relational model, SQL from joins to window functions, then the performance layer — indexes, plans, optimisation — and the NoSQL and analytics landscape beyond the single table.
for: Anyone learning SQL properly, and anyone who has been copying queries for years without knowing why they work.

name: Study That Sticks
blurb: The learning-science path: retrieval, spacing and deliberate practice first, then the memory and attention machinery, then the study systems — and the mindset that keeps them running when motivation does not.
for: Anyone studying for a certification or a new domain who wants the method, not just the material.

name: Frontend, From the Browser Up
blurb: How the web platform actually works, in build order: the render pipeline and the DOM, layout with grid and flexbox, the JavaScript that trips people up, a component framework, then the cross-cutting concerns — data, auth, security, performance, accessibility, testing and deploy.
for: Anyone moving from 'I can make it work' to understanding why, and anyone reviewing frontend code they did not write.

name: CS for Working Engineers
blurb: The computer-science a working engineer actually reaches for: complexity, the data structures and algorithms worth knowing cold, then how the machine runs them — scheduling, concurrency, memory — and the distributed-systems and latency facts that decide real designs.
for: Self-taught engineers filling the gaps, and anyone preparing for an interview that goes past framework trivia.

name: LLMs, From Prompt to Production
blurb: Building on large language models in the order the decisions arrive: what a model is and how a transformer works, then tokens and prompting, then giving it your own data with RAG, then making it act with tools and structured output, then the production concerns — cost, hallucination, injection, agent safety and shipping.
for: Engineers building with LLMs who want the mechanism and the failure modes, not just the API call.

name: Governance, Risk & Compliance, End to End
blurb: How a security programme is run and proven: risk from first principles, the frameworks and the controls universe, then classification and the audit, the major regimes (SOC 2, privacy law), third-party and continuity risk, and the governance machinery — the risk register, exceptions and reporting upward.
for: Anyone who has inherited 'compliance', and any engineer who wants to know what the auditors are actually asking for.

name: Ship It and Run It
blurb: The delivery loop end to end: how code leaves a branch, becomes an artifact, reaches production safely, and gets watched, answered for and learned from once it is live.
for: Engineers moving toward DevOps or SRE, and anyone who ships software but has never owned it in production.

name: Running Windows Server & Active Directory
blurb: The estate a Windows admin inherits, in the order it makes sense: the box, then the directory, then how changes travel, then policy, identity hygiene, the core services everything depends on, and what you do the day a domain controller dies.
for: Anyone handed a Windows estate, and anyone who has been clicking through AD without a model of what sits behind it.

name: The Layer Under Everything
blurb: Virtualisation, storage, clustering and backup — the platform every application quietly depends on, ending where it matters most: proving a restore actually works before you need it.
for: Anyone who owns hosts and arrays rather than apps, and any cloud engineer who wants to know what the abstraction is hiding.

name: From Engineer to Manager
blurb: The transition itself, then the job: the weekly loop of one-to-ones, delegation and feedback, building a team through hiring and onboarding, and the outward half nobody warns you about — planning, politics and reporting upward.
for: Engineers considering the move, anyone in their first year of it, and tech leads deciding whether they want it at all.

name: The Software Supply Chain
blurb: Everything that ends up in your build and how to prove where it came from: dependency risk, SBOM and VEX, SLSA levels, signing and attestation, verifying at deploy time, and the pipeline itself as an attack surface.
for: Engineers who own a build, and anyone asked to answer "are we affected?" with evidence rather than a guess.

name: Administering Microsoft 365
blurb: A tenant end to end: what you are actually looking at, who can change it, the object model underneath Teams and SharePoint, then mail, files, collaboration, the security baseline, compliance, and the triage order when something breaks.
for: Anyone handed a tenant, and anyone who administers one workload and wants the shape of the rest.

name: Running Azure
blurb: A subscription end to end: the hierarchy that governs it, the network and compute inside it, the identity layer that guards it, and the monitoring, automation and hybrid reach that keep it running.
for: Anyone administering Azure rather than just deploying to it, and Windows admins whose estate is now half in the cloud.

name: Securing Cloud-Native
blurb: Where the provider's responsibility ends and yours begins, then the whole attack surface of a container platform: identity and RBAC, workload isolation, exposure, serverless, and the detection and response that assume something already got in.
for: Engineers running Kubernetes or serverless in production, and security people who need the cloud control plane in their model.

name: Identity Is the Perimeter
blurb: How proof of who you are actually works, from factors and password storage through federation protocols and token lifetimes, then the attacks that target the identity layer itself — and the privilege, secrets and offboarding controls around it.
for: Anyone who owns authentication, and any engineer who has wired up OAuth without knowing what it promises.

name: Application & API Security
blurb: Model the threats, then meet the bug classes that keep appearing — injection, broken access control, the server-side heavy hitters — and follow them into APIs, where the web list stops being enough.
for: Developers who want to stop shipping the same bug classes, and anyone reviewing an application or an API for the first time.

name: Detection Engineering
blurb: Detections treated as software: a requirement before a rule, telemetry you proved exists, a schema, version control and tests — then the honest measurement of whether any of it works, and the discipline of retiring what does not.
for: SOC analysts moving into engineering the detections rather than answering them, and anyone who owns a rule set.

name: Digital Forensics & Incident Response
blurb: Evidence handling first, because everything after it depends on that being right — then the telemetry, the artifacts, and the disk, memory and at-scale tooling that reconstruct what actually happened.
for: Anyone who may have to answer "what did the attacker do?" with evidence that would survive scrutiny.

name: Penetration Testing, End to End
blurb: Authorisation first, then the phases in order — recon, scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation — and the half that decides whether the work was worth anything: rating findings honestly, writing the report, and disclosing responsibly.
for: Anyone working toward an authorised testing role, and defenders who want to understand the process being run against them.

name: Adversary Emulation & Purple Teaming
blurb: Emulation is not a pentest: you pick an adversary relevant to you, plan it with a kill switch, run it against your own detections, and measure what actually fired — then report it in a way that funds the next one.
for: Blue teams wanting to test their detections against real technique, and red teams moving from findings to measurable defensive improvement.

name: Python That Ships
blurb: The distance between a script that works on your machine and code someone else can install, run and trust: environments, errors and logging, typing and validation, CLIs, tests, tooling and packaging.
for: Anyone whose Python works but keeps breaking elsewhere, and scripters who want their tools used by other people.

name: Automation for Administrators
blurb: Scripting an estate rather than a laptop: PowerShell and Graph, scheduling that is safe to run twice, secrets that are never in the file, constrained remoting, config and images as code — and the blast-radius discipline that decides what you let it touch.
for: Sysadmins automating the repetitive parts of the job, and anyone whose scripts have started running unattended.

name: Linux Administration, Properly
blurb: Past the commands: the boot chain, who you actually are (sudoers and PAM), services and journald, storage and LVM, firewalls and mandatory access control, containers from their kernel primitives — and rescuing a box that will not boot.
for: Anyone responsible for Linux servers rather than just using one, and terminal-comfortable people who want the model underneath.

name: Reading the Threat Landscape
blurb: Who attacks, why, and how the economy behind it works — the frameworks for describing intrusions, the techniques that dominate real breaches, and the honest limits of attribution and intelligence.
for: Analysts who want context behind the alerts, and anyone briefing a business on what actually threatens it.

name: Endpoint Engineering with Intune
blurb: A modern Windows estate end to end: provisioning, policy and how to prove which one won, apps, the update rings, the security controls auditors ask about, and the compliance-to-Conditional-Access chain that makes a device trusted.
for: Intune engineers past the first ninety days, and anyone who owns device policy rather than just applying it.

name: The Mixed Fleet — Beyond Windows
blurb: Everything in the estate that is not a corporate Windows laptop: Macs, iOS and Android, personal devices you cannot demand root on, shared and kiosk hardware, sessions instead of endpoints, and the browser that is really the most-used app you manage.
for: Windows-shop admins meeting Apple and mobile for the first time, and anyone writing a BYOD policy that has to survive contact.

name: Running MECM (ConfigMgr)
blurb: The on-prem half of endpoint management: what the product is, the architecture decisions that decide whether the site server survives, the log maps for site and client health, deployment and OSD triage — and the co-management path out.
for: Anyone who inherited a ConfigMgr hierarchy, and cloud-first admins who still have one to keep alive.

name: Hardware & the Bench
blurb: From the electrical basics up to a machine that will not POST: what the components do, what the test gear tells you, and the isolate-and-swap discipline that finds a fault instead of guessing at one.
for: Field techs and repair benches, A+ candidates, and anyone who builds or fixes their own machines.

name: Going Independent
blurb: The business behind the technical work: which model you are actually in, how to price it, how to scope it so the first two weeks don't eat the margin, how to report it — and how to grow past selling your own hours.
for: Engineers considering consulting or contracting, and independents who are good at the work and losing money on the rest.

name: Teaching & Enablement
blurb: Explaining things so they land: how adults actually learn, sequencing a curriculum, running a room, demoing without disaster, and the written artefacts — docs, diagrams, proposals — that teach when you are not there.
for: Anyone who trains, onboards, runs workshops, or writes the documentation everyone else relies on.

name: Sustaining a Long Career
blurb: The part of the job nobody schedules: imposter feelings and comparison, motivation and failure, burnout and the always-on feeling, the pager, the body you sit in, a manager you cannot fix — and knowing when the answer is professional help.
for: Anyone planning to still be doing this in ten years, and anyone who is not sure they can keep going at this pace.

name: Observability, Properly
blurb: From "we have dashboards" to knowing what to instrument, what each signal is bad at, and what the bill will be.
for: Engineers and SREs who own a system in production

name: Running a Service Desk
blurb: The craft nobody writes down: the queue, the ticket, the escalation, the metrics that improve service and the ones that only look good.
for: Service desk staff, team leads, and anyone who owns a support queue

name: Designing for Failure
blurb: Everything fails. The route from that sentence to bulkheads, load shedding, gamedays and a recovery capability you have actually tested.
for: Architects and operators of systems that are expected to stay up

name: Thinking Clearly
blurb: Arguments, evidence, models and the traps in your own head — the reasoning kit underneath every technical decision.
for: Anyone who has to decide something with incomplete information

name: Building an Internal Platform
blurb: The honest version: why the role exists, the thinnest thing that works, and how to tell whether anyone is using it.
for: Platform teams, and the engineering leads deciding whether to fund one

name: The Modern Data Stack
blurb: Ingest, warehouse, model, test, orchestrate — analytics engineering as an engineering discipline, and what it costs.
for: Analytics engineers and anyone who owns a warehouse

name: AI Safety, Security & Governance
blurb: The other half of shipping AI: what attacks it, what it leaks, what you owe the people it affects, and the policy that survives contact.
for: Anyone putting a model in front of real users or real data

name: From the Military to IT
blurb: What transfers, what needs translating, and the paperwork and timing that decide how the transition actually goes.
for: Service leavers and veterans moving into technology

name: Handling Classified Material
blurb: Markings, forms, containers and the first ten minutes of a spill — the procedural half of a cleared role, in order.
for: Anyone newly cleared, or supporting a classified environment

name: Cryptography, End to End
blurb: From what a hash is to reading a vendor's crypto claim critically — including the maths that makes it hard and the migration that is already overdue.
for: Engineers and security staff who need to choose, deploy or defend crypto

name: Distributed Systems, From First Principles
blurb: Why the hard parts are hard: time you cannot trust, failures you cannot detect, and agreement you have to pay for.
for: Engineers building or operating anything that spans more than one machine

name: The Maths Under the Job
blurb: The small amount of probability and statistics that decides whether a detection, a dashboard or an experiment means anything.
for: Anyone who reports a number and would rather it were true

name: How Your Code Actually Runs
blurb: Source to silicon: compilers, interpreters, types, collectors, pipelines — and the security bugs that live in the gaps.
for: Engineers who want the layer below the language they write

name: Privacy & Data Protection, in Practice
blurb: Past the policy PDF: where personal data actually is, how to delete it for real, and what a subject access request costs you.
for: Engineers and privacy staff who have to make the law true in a system

name: Programming From Zero
blurb: The whole beginner curriculum in order — from what a bit is to reading a complete program and understanding every line.
for: Anyone learning to code, with no assumptions and nothing skipped

name: The Concepts Behind the Code
blurb: The vocabulary and the reasoning a self-taught developer is missing — objects, structures, complexity, patterns and the shape of an API.
for: Anyone comfortable writing code and unsure what the words in job adverts mean

name: Designing Software That Lasts
blurb: Architecture as a series of trade-offs you can name: what to split, what to couple, what to make resilient, and how to argue for it.
for: Engineers moving from writing features to shaping systems

name: The Money Side of IT
blurb: Budgets, business cases, vendors and contracts — the half of a senior technical job that nobody teaches and everybody is judged on.
for: Technical leads, managers and anyone who has to ask for money or sign something

name: Running an Enterprise Network
blurb: Ports, loops, routes, firewalls and the cutover night — the day job of a network engineer, in the order the problems arrive.
for: Network engineers and the infrastructure staff who inherit the network

name: Wireless, Properly
blurb: Radio is a shared medium and most Wi-Fi complaints are physics — channels, surveys, roaming and the operating model you chose.
for: Anyone who owns a wireless network and hears that it is slow

name: The Protocols You Actually Meet
blurb: What is really happening on the wire: addressing, name resolution, the web's transport, and the tunnels and proxies in between.
for: Engineers who read packet captures and want the protocols behind them

name: The Offensive Toolkit, By Phase
blurb: The tools in the order an engagement uses them — recon, scan, web, exploit, credentials, C2, lateral, exfil — each with what it needs first.
for: Testers and defenders who want the catalogue as a chain rather than a list

name: Ransomware, End to End
blurb: How it gets in, how the business around it works, what negotiation actually looks like, and the backup design that decides the outcome.
for: Anyone who will be in the room when it happens

name: AWS, End to End
blurb: Account structure first, then identity, network, compute, storage, data, security, IaC and observability — the order that avoids rework.
for: Anyone learning or inheriting an AWS estate

name: Google Cloud, End to End
blurb: The resource hierarchy decides everything else — then identity, network, compute, data, security and the KRM way of describing it all.
for: Anyone learning or inheriting a GCP estate

name: The Cloud Bill and the Contract
blurb: Tagging you can enforce, commitments you can forecast, quotas that cause outages, residency you must prove, and the door you should price early.
for: Anyone accountable for what the cloud costs or where the data sits

name: Security for Everyone
blurb: No jargon, no assumed background: what the threats actually are, what to do about them, and why the advice is what it is.
for: Anyone who uses a computer for work and has never been taught this

name: The Modern Security Edge
blurb: What replaced the perimeter: segmentation, zero trust, ZTNA, SASE and the SaaS visibility problem underneath the acronyms.
for: Security and network staff redesigning access for people who are not in the building

name: Knowing Your Own Attack Surface
blurb: Find what you actually expose before somebody else does — assets, domains, certificates, leaked credentials and impersonation.
for: Security teams who need an inventory before they need a control

name: Security Where There Is Hardware
blurb: OT, ICS, firmware, badges and physical access — the environments where the generic answer is the wrong one and consequence is measured differently.
for: Anyone securing plant, devices or a building rather than a data centre

name: The Insider, and the Investigation
blurb: The threat with legitimate access, and how to look into it without becoming the problem — evidence, lanes and the line you must not cross.
for: Security, HR-adjacent and investigation staff

name: Linux, From Newcomer to Confident
blurb: The first six months: the shell, files and permissions, packages, processes, services, scripts and the containers everyone will hand you.
for: Anyone meeting Linux for the first time, or the first time seriously

name: Running Linux Servers
blurb: Storage, sharing, mail, availability and the boot-integrity chain — the services a Linux estate actually runs, and how each one fails.
for: Linux administrators past the basics

name: Choosing and Running a Database
blurb: Which engine, and then the operational half nobody demos: pooling, locking, partitioning, replication, backups and what to watch.
for: Engineers who own a database rather than just query one

name: The Frontend That Ships
blurb: Past the framework: rendering modes, data fetching, realtime, forms, theming, i18n, accessibility remediation and the SEO nobody owns.
for: Frontend engineers responsible for a real product

name: The Microsoft 365 Workloads
blurb: Past the tenant: mail, Teams voice, the migrations, the small apps with data nobody governs, and the hybrid you did not mean to keep.
for: M365 administrators past the identity and policy basics

name: The Frameworks, and the Audit
blurb: Which framework applies, what it actually requires, and how to be ready for the auditor without a three-week fire drill.
for: Anyone who has been handed a compliance obligation

name: How Models Actually Work
blurb: From what machine learning is to KV caches and multi-agent hand-offs — the mechanism under the tools, in order.
for: Anyone who wants the internals rather than the API surface

name: AI at Work
blurb: Using it well yourself, then deploying it for other people — licensing, data boundaries and the assistant everyone already turned on.
for: IT staff who have to make AI useful and safe for a whole organisation

name: First Steps in Offensive Security
blurb: The beginner route, with authorisation first: the method, the lab, recon, the first web bug, privilege escalation and how to report it.
for: Anyone starting out in ethical hacking

name: The Blue Team Toolkit
blurb: The defensive stack tool by tool — capture, metadata, signatures, SIEM, fleet queries, intel platforms, hardening scanners and deception.
for: SOC analysts and defenders building or inheriting the stack

name: Kubernetes, End to End
blurb: Containers, then the objects, then packaging, networking, storage, security — and the parts that decide what happens under pressure.
for: Engineers running workloads on Kubernetes

name: Getting Your Time Back
blurb: Inbox, goals, weekly review, focus blocks and the failure modes of every system you have already abandoned once.
for: Anyone whose week runs them rather than the other way round

name: Malware, and the Attack Itself
blurb: What the code does, how it hides, how attacks are modelled, and the parts of the ecosystem that decide who gets hit.
for: Analysts and engineers who want the attack side without the tooling

name: Building a Career That Compounds
blurb: The things that pay off slowly: a lab, a reputation, relationships, certifications chosen deliberately, and money that works while you do.
for: Anyone who has the technical skills and wants the rest of it

name: The Maths Behind Machine Learning
blurb: Vectors, matrices, gradients and loss — the small set of ideas that makes an embedding, a GPU and a training run make sense.
for: Engineers who use models and want the mechanism underneath

name: The Estate Nobody Documented
blurb: Legacy directories, ageing certificate authorities, tape nobody has restored, mainframes and the servers you must decommission properly.
for: Anyone who has just inherited an environment older than their tenure

name: Delivery Pipelines in Practice
blurb: The concrete half of CI/CD: the platforms, the workflow files, the artifacts, the config management and the release note people read.
for: Engineers wiring up the pipeline rather than reasoning about flow

name: Radio, Wireless & Physical Tooling
blurb: The offensive hardware and RF side, and the cloud attack surface that sits beside it — each with what it needs before it does anything.
for: Testers working beyond the network cable, and the defenders opposite them

name: Reading Military Structure
blurb: Staff codes, prefixes, functional numbers and echelons — how to read an organisation chart that looks like a licence plate.
for: Anyone working with or joining a military or defence organisation

name: Hardware Beyond the PC
blurb: Boards, buses, firmware and real-time constraints — plus the conference room and the accessibility kit that are also hardware problems.
for: Anyone whose work touches devices rather than servers
